title: pressed other believers.
paragraphs: pressed other believers.
They had done things that looked extraordinary.
But something was terribly wrong beneath everything that looked spiritually impressive.
And the question that should haunt us is not simply, “Who are these people?”
The question is…
What if I have become so familiar with Christianity that I have stopped examining whether I am actually following Christ?
Because it is possible to know the language of salvation without understanding the surrender of salvation.
It is possible to defend biblical truth publicly while privately resisting the very truth we defend.
It is possible to sing about the holiness of God on Sunday and spend the rest of the week protecting sins we refuse to bring into His light.
It is possible to love the atmosphere of church without loving the authority of Jesus.
And perhaps the most dangerous spiritual condition is not knowing that you are lost.
Perhaps it is being so convinced that you are safe that you no longer listen when Scripture calls you to examine your heart.
But before this becomes a weapon pointed at someone else, allow the Word of God to turn the question toward us.
Not your pastor.
Not the person sitting across the aisle.
Not that Christian who disappointed you.
You.
Me.
All of us.
Because Jesus did not give this warning so that we could become experts at identifying false believers.
He gave it so that we would stop confusing religious appearance with genuine discipleship.
And there is something even more astonishing hidden in His words.
In the original Greek of Matthew 7:23, Jesus says:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
Oudépote égnōn hymâs.
“I never knew you.”
The word οὐδέποτε means “never,” and ἔγνων comes from the verb γινώσκω, meaning “to know.”
In this context, Jesus is not suggesting that He lacked information about these people.
He knew who they were.
He knew their actions.
He knew their hearts.
The statement concerns the absence of a genuine relationship of belonging to Him.
Notice that He does not say, “I knew you once, but then I forgot you.”
He says, “I never knew you.”

This passage should not be carelessly used to settle every theological debate about whether salvation can be lost. Christians have understood that broader question differently. But the immediate warning is unmistakable: an impressive religious profession, even accompanied by extraordinary claims, does not by itself establish that someone belongs to Christ.
That distinction is terrifying.
And merciful.
Terrifying because religious confidence can be misplaced.
Merciful because Jesus is warning us now, while there is still time to hear His voice.
Imagine a man who has attended church for thirty years.
He knows exactly when to stand.
He knows when to bow his head.
He knows which worship songs make people cry.
He can quote Scripture from memory.
His Bible is worn. His Sunday clothes are pressed. His reputation is spotless.
People call him a pillar of the church.
But at home, his wife has learned to recognize the sound of his footsteps because she never knows which version of him will walk through the door.
His children know the man who prays beautifully in public.
They also know the man who humiliates them behind closed doors.
He gives generously when others are watching, but refuses to apologize when he wounds someone.
He can identify false doctrine in seconds, but cannot admit when his own pride has become an idol.
And when confronted, he says the same thing he has said for years.
“I've been a Christian longer than you've been alive.”
As though time spent near holy things automatically makes a heart holy.
As though a lifetime of church attendance can substitute for repentance.
As though knowing the right answers means we have surrendered to the One who is the Truth.
Now imagine another person.
A woman sitting near the back of the sanctuary.
She barely raises her hands during worship.
She struggles to pray because shame keeps interrupting her thoughts.
Her past is complicated.
Her faith sometimes trembles.
She knows she has made decisions she cannot undo.
She has no impressive ministry title, no public platform, and no polished testimony.
But when she hears the Gospel, something in her breaks.
Not because she thinks she is better than anyone.
But because she knows she desperately needs mercy.
And through tears, she whispers:
“Jesus, I have nothing to offer You except the truth about who I am. Please have mercy on me.”
Which person looks more spiritual?
And which one is responding to the grace of God?
We cannot see either person's heart perfectly. But Jesus told a parable that exposes the danger of trusting religious performance.
In Luke 18:9–14, a Pharisee and a tax collector went to the temple to pray.
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other sinners.
He listed his fasting and tithing.
His prayer was full of religious achievement.
The tax collector, however, stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beat his breast and cried:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” (Luke 18:13, KJV).
Jesus said the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee.
The religious man trusted in his own righteousness.
The broken man appealed to God's mercy.
And heaven's verdict was the opposite of what many observers might have expected.
There is a Hebrew word that helps illuminate the mercy the tax collector desperately needed.
חֶסֶד — ḥésed
It is often translated as “mercy,” “steadfast love,” or “lovingkindness,” depending on its context.
In passages such as Psalm 51:1, it describes the faithful mercy David pleaded for after his sin was exposed.
But the tax collector's actual prayer in Luke 18 was recorded in Greek, using the verb ἱλάσθητί, an appeal for God to be merciful or gracious toward him.
These are not identical words, and we should not pretend they are.
Yet both passages reveal the same desperate human need.
A sinner cannot purchase forgiveness with religious achievements.
He must receive mercy from God.
And that mercy is not cheap.
It leads us to the cross.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that God has lowered His standards so that religious people can feel comfortable.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again, accomplishing what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV).
Did you catch that?
Not of works.
Not of titles.
Not of church attendance.
Not of ministry accomplishments.
Not of the number of people who applaud your testimony.
Not of how much money you give.
Not even of how long you have called yourself a Christian.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And genuine saving faith does not leave us indifferent to the One who saved us.
The very next verse says that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10).
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are part of the fruit of a life transformed by grace.
That is why the warning of Jesus matters so much.
He is not condemning people for failing to accumulate enough religious achievements.
He is exposing the tragedy of people who appeal to religious achievements while remaining strangers to genuine obedience and relationship with Him.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because most of us are not tempted to announce, “I hate Jesus.”
We are tempted to say, “I love Jesus,” while quietly reserving certain rooms of our lives where we do not want Him to enter.
We want His peace, but not His correction.
His promises, but not His commands.
His forgiveness, but not the uncomfortable work of confessing what we have done.
His blessing, but not the humility of surrender.
We want a Savior who rescues us from judgment, but sometimes resist the Lord who calls us to turn away from the very sins that are destroying us.
And when someone lovingly confronts us with Scripture, we can become more offended by the correction than grieved by the sin.
That is when religion becomes dangerous.
Not because church attendance is wrong.
Not because serving in ministry is wrong.
Not because preaching, teaching, worshiping, or giving are wrong.
Those things can be beautiful expressions of genuine faith.
But when they become substitutes for repentance, humility, love, and obedience, they can create a frightening illusion of spiritual health.
Jesus spoke to this problem in Revelation 3.
The church in Laodicea believed it was rich and needed nothing.
But Christ exposed its spiritual poverty.
They were satisfied with themselves while failing to recognize their true condition.
And yet, listen to the mercy in His warning.
“As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.” (Revelation 3:19, KJV).
He did not expose them because He delighted in humiliating them. He called them to repentance because His rebuke was an expression of love.
That changes everything.
Conviction is not always evidence that God is pushing you away.
Sometimes it is the very means by which He is calling you back to the truth.
The fact that Scripture unsettles you does not automatically mean your faith is false.
A tender conscience can be a beautiful thing.
A believer who grieves over sin and returns to Christ is not the same as a person who deliberately uses religion to excuse unrepentant evil.
Even genuine Christians struggle.
Even mature believers need correction.
Even faithful disciples sometimes stumble terribly.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Think about that.
The man who had walked with Christ, heard His teaching, witnessed His miracles, and confessed Him as the Messiah stood in a courtyard and denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter remembered.
Luke 22:62 tells us:
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.”
Can you imagine those tears?
The sound of his own voice still echoing in his memory.
The shame of knowing he had denied the One he promised never to abandon.
The awful realization that courage had disappeared when it mattered most.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, the risen Christ asked Peter three times whether he loved Him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The restoration was not a denial of what Peter had done.
It was grace meeting a broken disciple and calling him forward.
That is the difference between a Gospel of grace and a religion of appearances.
Religion says, “Hide your failure so people will continue to respect you.”
Grace says, “Bring your failure into the light because Jesus is able to restore you.”
Religion says, “Protect your reputation.”
Grace says, “Tell the truth.”
Religion says, “You must appear strong.”
Grace says, “Christ's strength is made perfect in weakness.”
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years pretending.
You smile when someone asks how your walk with God is going.
You say, “I'm blessed.”
But behind that smile is a private battle.
Maybe pornography has become a secret prison.
Maybe bitterness has been living in your heart for so long that you no longer recognize it as bitterness.
Maybe you have wounded people and justified it because you were wounded first.
Maybe your marriage is collapsing while everyone at church assumes you are a beautiful Christian family.
Maybe you are exhausted from performing spirituality.
Maybe you can quote the promises of God but have not spoken honestly to Him in months.
Or maybe you have been living in quiet fear, wondering whether you are truly saved because you still struggle with sin.
Please hear this carefully.
The answer is not to become obsessed with proving that you are good enough for Jesus.
You are not saved by achieving moral perfection.
The answer is to turn toward Jesus Himself.
Confess what is true.
Stop defending what Scripture calls sin.
Trust what Christ accomplished through His death and resurrection.
Ask Him to transform the places you have kept hidden.
And when you fall, do not run farther into darkness.
Return to the Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια — metánoia.
It speaks of a change of mind or understanding, and in the biblical call to repentance, that inward change is expressed in turning toward God and away from sin.
It is not merely feeling bad because you were caught.
It is not crying during a worship song and then deliberately returning to the same rebellion without concern.
It is not promising God you will never struggle again.
It is a real turning of the heart toward Him, a turning that bears fruit over time.
And even repentance is not a trophy we place before God to boast about ourselves.
It is a response to His truth and grace.
That is why 2 Corinthians 13:5 is so important:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” (KJV).
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “Spend the rest of your life terrified that every weakness proves you are condemned.”
He calls believers to examine themselves.
To take faith seriously.
To refuse empty assumptions.
To recognize the reality of Christ's presence and work among them.
Healthy self-examination should drive us toward truth, repentance, and dependence on Jesus—not into endless spiritual panic.
And if you are wondering whether your faith is real, do not begin by comparing yourself to the most impressive Christian you know.
Begin with Christ.
Do you believe the Gospel?
Are you trusting Him rather than your own righteousness?
When His Word exposes sin, do you ultimately want to defend that sin or turn from it?
Is there evidence, however imperfect and growing, that His grace is changing your life?
Do you love Him, even when your love feels painfully weak?
And when you fail, where do you run?
Toward the cross?
Or deeper into the disguise?
These questions are not a mechanical test that can reveal everything about the human heart.
Only God knows us perfectly.
But they can help expose the difference between resting in Christ and resting in a religious identity.
Because there is another danger we must confront.
Sometimes the person most eager to call everyone else a false Christian is avoiding examination of their own soul.
They see hypocrisy everywhere except in the mirror.
They have turned discernment into contempt.
They use the truth as a hammer against wounded people while refusing to let that same truth correct their own pride.
And this too is dangerous.
Jesus warned against judging others hypocritically while ignoring the beam in our own eye (Matthew 7:1–5).
Biblical discernment matters.
Church accountability matters.
Sound doctrine matters.
But none of those gives us permission to act as though we can see the final condition of another person's soul.
The purpose of this message is not to create a new generation of suspicious Christians who spend their days deciding who is saved.
It is to call us to become honest disciples who take Jesus seriously.
A church filled with humble believers who confess sin, practice love, seek justice, extend forgiveness, protect the vulnerable, and submit to Scripture is a powerful witness to the Gospel.
A church filled with people protecting religious appearances at any cost can become a place where hypocrisy flourishes and wounded souls learn to suffer silently.
That is why the most dangerous kind of religious confidence is confidence that no longer listens to correction.
It does not merely damage the person who carries it.
It can damage families.
It can silence victims.
It can discourage seekers.
It can make unbelievers associate the name of Jesus with arrogance rather than grace.
And it can teach the next generation to imitate Christian performance instead of Christian discipleship.
But Jesus is not asking His church to become a theater of perfect people.
He is calling us to become a people who live in the truth.
People who repent.
People who forgive.
People who admit when they are wrong.
People who do not use grace as permission to continue in sin.
People who do not use holiness as an excuse for cruelty.
People who know that without Christ, they have nothing to boast about.
And perhaps this is the moment to ask a question that is harder than any theological debate.
If nobody at church knew your name, your position, your giving history, or your ministry accomplishments, would Jesus still be the treasure of your heart?
Not because your emotions are always strong.
Not because your obedience is flawless.
But because you have come to understand that He is not an accessory to your identity.
He is your life.
There is a beautiful statement in Philippians 3:8, where Paul speaks of counting everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord.
Paul had religious credentials.
He had zeal.
He had status.
He had reasons, humanly speaking, to boast.
But after encountering Christ, he understood that his standing before God could not rest on his own righteousness.
He wanted to be found in Christ, having righteousness through faith in Him (Philippians 3:9).
This is the heart of genuine Christianity.
Not merely knowing things about Jesus.
But belonging to Jesus.
Not performing for acceptance.
But being transformed by the grace we have received.
Not using religion to hide our sins.
But bringing them to the Savior who died to redeem sinners.
And there is something profoundly hopeful here.
If this message has exposed something in you, the invitation is not to despair.
It is to come to Christ.
Today.
Not when you have cleaned up every part of your life.
Not when your emotions become perfectly stable.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Jesus said:
“All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV).
That is not a reluctant Savior speaking.
That is Jesus.
The same Jesus who warned about false profession also promised to receive those who come to Him.
The same Jesus who confronted hypocrisy also welcomed repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who exposed darkness gave His life to bring people into the light.
His warnings are real.
His holiness is real.
His judgment is real.
But so are His mercy, His forgiveness, and His power to save.
And if you are afraid because you know how far you have wandered, remember this:
The cross is not proof that your sin was insignificant.
It is proof that God's love moved toward sinners at immeasurable cost.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our religious image.
He came to save us.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He is alive.
And He is worthy of more than a Sunday identity.
He is worthy of our trust.
Our obedience.
Our worship.
Our whole lives.
So perhaps tonight, before you sleep, there is a conversation you need to have with God.
No audience.
No microphone.
No carefully chosen Christian phrases.
Just honesty.

“Lord Jesus, You know me better than I know myself. You know the parts of my life I show people and the parts I try to hide. Forgive my sins. Expose the pride I have defended. Break the power of the habits that keep pulling me away from You. Teach me to trust Your grace instead of my religious reputation. Give me a heart that loves what You love and turns away from what dishonors You. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I need You, Jesus. Not just as part of my life, but as my Savior and Lord. Make me genuine. Make me humble. Make me Yours. Amen.”
And if you have prayed something like that sincerely, remember that salvation does not depend on the exact wording of a prayer.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ.
Keep coming to Him.
Open His Word.
Seek fellowship with believers who will speak truth in love.
Find mature, trustworthy Christian leaders who can walk with you in discipleship.
Make amends where appropriate and safe.
And when repentance requires a difficult change, take the next faithful step.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic testimony to prove that God is working.
Sometimes transformation begins quietly.
With an apology you have avoided.
A secret sin brought into the light.
A decision to stop lying.
A willingness to seek help.
A Bible opened again after months of silence.
A wounded believer daring to trust Christ again.
Or a proud Christian finally whispering:
“Lord, I was wrong.”
That may never become a viral moment.
But heaven does not measure spiritual transformation by social media applause.
And that brings me to something deeply personal about why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want to keep pointing people to the living Christ.
To open Scripture.
To confront spiritual complacency without crushing the brokenhearted.
To remind exhausted believers of grace.
To help seekers understand the Gospel.
To encourage genuine repentance, healing, restoration, and daily discipleship.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is sitting alone with questions they are afraid to ask.
Someone is wondering whether Jesus could forgive what they have done.
Someone has been wounded by religious hypocrisy and is struggling to separate the failures of Christians from the goodness of Christ.
Someone is one honest conversation away from admitting that their spiritual life has become a performance.
And perhaps the words you share today could help that person open a Bible, seek prayer, return to fellowship, or turn toward Jesus.

Send it privately to a friend or family member who needs encouragement, especially someone who has been wounded by religion and needs to hear that Jesus is not the same as the hypocrisy they experienced.
And please, do not leave this conversation without considering the question at its center.
If Jesus examined your heart today, what is one thing you know you need to surrender to Him?
You do not have to disclose private details or expose wounds that are not safe to share publicly.

And if Christ has brought you out of religious performance into a deeper understanding of His grace, consider sharing a short testimony. Someone reading the comments may need to know that restoration is possible.
Your honesty could encourage another person to stop pretending.
And if you are ready to go deeper, I want to invite you into something more than another social media feed.
We want these resources to continue reaching people who need biblical truth and encouragement, including those who may not have the means to purchase Christian books or study materials.
You do not have to give money to earn His blessing.
And you should never feel pressured to give beyond what you can responsibly afford.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving should come from a willing heart, not from compulsion.
Not merely as someone who enjoys an article.
But as a partner who wants sound biblical encouragement and discipleship resources to keep reaching more people.
It is the opportunity to participate in a mission that seeks to keep Jesus Christ at the center.
Recommend the free library to a friend who is hungry for Scripture.
Pray that every message we publish will be faithful to God's Word.
It must be measured by faithfulness to Christ and His Gospel.
And that brings us back to the sentence where this all began.
“I never knew you.”
There are few words more sobering.
But there is another biblical truth that deserves to be remembered beside them.
“The Lord knoweth them that are his.” (2 Timothy 2:19, KJV).
What a comfort for those who truly belong to Christ.
He knows His sheep.
He calls them by name.
They hear His voice and follow Him.
He gives them eternal life, and no one can snatch them out of His hand (John 10:27–29).
Our assurance is not built on pretending we never struggle.
It is built on the faithful Savior who keeps His promises.
So do not leave this article merely frightened of being exposed.
Leave it willing to be honest.
Do not spend your life collecting Christian accomplishments while neglecting communion with Christ.
Do not confuse conviction with condemnation, or grace with permission to sin.
Do not mistake a wounded believer who is fighting to follow Jesus for a hypocrite who refuses to repent.
And do not become so busy identifying the spiritual blindness of others that you forget your own daily need for mercy.
There is still grace for the repentant.
Still forgiveness in Christ.
Still hope for the exhausted.
Still restoration for the fallen.
Still power in the Gospel to transform a life that has been built on appearances.
The religious mask can come off.
The hidden sin can be confessed.
The proud heart can bow.
The wandering believer can return.
The sinner can come to Jesus.
And the story that seemed destined to end in shame can become a testimony of His mercy.
Because that is what the Gospel does.
It does not pretend the scandal never happened.
It reveals a Savior whose grace is greater than the sinner's ability to repair the past.
It does not merely change what people call us.
Through Christ, it changes who we are becoming.
And one day, when all the titles, applause, public ministries, and carefully maintained appearances have faded away, only one thing will matter above everything else.
Not whether the church knew your name.
Not whether the world admired your faith.
Not whether your religious achievements impressed anyone.
But whether you truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
The greatest tragedy would not be walking into church with a broken past—it would be spending your whole life hiding behind a holy appearance while refusing the Savior who came to make you new.
